Article Title: SpaceX's Starship reaches orbit on its 14th flight after engine scare; company says: The team has made the call not to...
Article Text:
SpaceX's mega rocket Starship makes a test flight from Starbase, Texas, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Eric Gay)

Starlink V3 satellites become Starship's first real payload

Reaching orbit keeps Starship on track for NASA's Artemis moon missions

SpaceX's Starship has finally reached orbit. The world's largest and most powerful rocket lifted off from the company's Starbase facility in Texas at 7:48am local time on Monday (6:18pm IST). On its 14th test flight, Starship circled the Earth for the first time instead of briefly touching space and falling back.It nearly didn't happen. Shortly after the upper stage separated from its Super Heavy booster, one of Starship's engines shut down too early. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot told viewers on the live stream that the team had decided not to commit to orbit. Minutes later, engineers confirmed the ship could still perform the burn it needed. It did, and Mission Control announced "Starship is orbital" to loud cheers at the launch site.Once in orbit at an altitude of about 275km, Starship released 26 Starlink V3 satellites one at a time. Musk later posted on X that all 26 were deployed and operating normally.These satellites can each handle about 10 times more data than the V2 Mini units SpaceX currently launches on Falcon 9. The company says a single full Starship launch of V3 satellites adds as much network capacity as 20 Falcon 9 flights.The new satellites should start serving Starlink customers within weeks.The flight did not run its full course, though. SpaceX had planned six laps around the planet over nearly 10 hours, ending with a splashdown near Chile. About 90 minutes in, the company said it would deorbit the ship after roughly three hours. It gave no reason for the change. Starship came down north of Hawaii, flipped upright just before hitting the water, then tipped over and burst into flames. SpaceX had never planned to recover it.The booster dropped into the Gulf of Mexico for an engine-controlled splashdown, though SpaceX said some of its engines cut out on the way down. The booster had made hard landings on the two previous flights.Musk once expected Starship to reach orbit by 2022. All 13 earlier flights were suborbital, and the programme has cost SpaceX more than $15 billion (roughly Rs 1.3 lakh crore). NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated the company on the result.The timing matters for NASA. Artemis III, planned for as early as next summer, will test Starship docking with an Orion capsule in Earth orbit. Artemis IV, due no sooner than 2028, will land astronauts on the Moon using either Starship or Jeff Bezos' Blue Moon, depending on which is ready first.Next, SpaceX wants to catch a returning Starship with the launch tower's mechanical arms. Musk rates the chances as even or slightly better. If the catch works, the same ship could fly again by the end of the year or early next year.SpaceX shares slipped about 1% on Monday after the early return was announced. Still, the flight survived an engine failure, delivered a working payload and came down where it was meant to. For a rocket whose test flights exploded over the Bahamas and spun out of control last year, that counts as solid progress.
Article Summary: World's largest and most powerful rocket lifted off from the company's Starbase facility in Texas. On its 14th test flight, Starship circled the Earth for the first time instead of briefly touching space and falling back. Starship released 26 Starlink V3 satellites one at a time.

Article Title: After Jensen Huang warned ChatGPT maker OpenAI and other companies to shut down models they can’t make safe, Nvidia launches software to stop AI agents from going rogue
Article Text:
Representative Image

Nvidia launches tools to contain AI agents

“Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can’t govern what agents can access or do,”

Nvidia says its software could have stopped OpenAI incident

“Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail,”

“From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks.”

Jensen Huang's warning to AI labs

“You have to think about what you could have done, what’s the solution for it,”

“In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again.”

“Now, if they say the alternative, which is: There is no way to contain our experiments, there’s just no way; when we test our A.I. models, it will get out, and it will damage the world — then I think the answer is that we have to shut the labs down,” h

“Don’t ship the product. If your product is not ready to ship, don’t ship the product,”

Nvidia is rolling out new software to prevent AI agents from escaping controlled environments and accessing systems they aren't supposed to reach. The launch comes soon after CEO Jensen Huang warned that AI labs should not continue operating if they cannot contain their experiments. Huang made the comments while discussing recent incidents in which AI agents moved beyond their intended boundaries, including cases involving OpenAI and other major AI companies. However, during his interview, Huang didn’t specifically mention the ChatGPT maker, in which Nvidia has already invested billionsNvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform is now being positioned as an engineering solution to that problem, giving developers tools to limit what AI agents can access and do. The company says the platform could have prevented OpenAI’s July incident involving Hugging Face, when models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and attacked the open-source developer platform. Here is how Nvidia’s new safety system works and why Huang’s warning matters.Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform is designed to add controls around AI agents as they perform tasks. The company says recent incidents show that model-level safeguards alone may not be enough to control what agents can access once they operate independently.said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia.One part of the platform is Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and is designed to limit an agent’s capabilities. Nvidia has also introduced Sentry, a monitoring system that runs on network chips rather than CPUs or GPUs.Nvidia describes the platform as a reference design, with some components open source. The approach allows other companies to build products and services around the technology rather than treating it as a single finished product.Nvidia’s announcement follows several incidents involving AI agents operating outside their intended environments. An Nvidia representative said the new platform could have prevented OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident in July.According to Boitano, Hugging Face reported more than 17,000 agents attacking its infrastructure over a period that lasted days and weeks.Boitano said.The incidents have increased attention on how AI agents should be contained as they become capable of browsing the internet, using software and interacting with external systems.Huang discussed the issue in a recent conversation with The New York Times’ Ezra Klein, arguing that AI safety should be approached as an engineering and product-development problem.Huang said.Huang also gave a conditional warning about AI labs that cannot control their experiments.e added.He also argued that companies should not release systems that are not ready.Huang said.His comments came as companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google have disclosed incidents involving AI systems and controlled testing environments.
Article Summary: N Nvidia is rolling out new software to prevent AI agents from escaping controlled environments and accessing systems they aren't supposed to reach. CEO Jensen Huang warned that AI labs should not continue operating if they cannot contain their experiments. Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform is designed to add controls around AI agents as they perform tasks.

Article Title: When a district in Florida used robot rabbits to eliminate growing population of Burmese pythons and protect Everglades
Article Text:
How Florida’s AI-powered robot rabbits work

PC: AI Generated

Why Florida is targeting Burmese pythons

Florida Python Challenge adds to python removal efforts

“The Florida Python Challenge shows what is possible when we all come together around a shared conservation goal,”

Florida used an unusual tool to control the growing population of invasive Burmese pythons in the Everglades: solar-powered robot rabbits. In 2025, the South Florida Water Management District and the University of Florida teamed up to deploy robotic rabbit decoys designed to mimic real prey and lure pythons out of hiding using artificial intelligence (AI), heat signatures and scent simulation.The robots are part of Florida’s broader effort to remove Burmese pythons, which have disrupted native wildlife populations across the state. The devices use AI-powered cameras to detect approaching snakes and alert officials, who can then send trained python removal agents to capture and remove them. The technology is being used alongside the annual Florida Python Challenge and other removal programmes, not replacing them. The initiative reflects a growing shift toward integrating robotics and machine learning into wildlife management, offering conservationists a scalable alternative to manual patrols across swampland. Researchers say the robotic rabbits could transform python detection, letting officials monitor remote wetlands continuously while reducing risky manual searches and helping protect the Everglades' struggling native mammals, birds, and reptiles.The solar-powered robots are designed to imitate prey that Burmese pythons hunt. They produce a heat signature and emit a scent intended to attract the snakes, which use thermal sensing and smell while hunting. Each robot has an AI-powered camera that monitors the surrounding area. When it detects a python approaching, the system alerts South Florida Water Management District officials. A trained python removal agent can then be dispatched to the location.Because the robots are solar-powered, they can remain in remote wetland areas for extended periods without requiring a conventional power supply. The system is designed to turn a python’s approach into an alert for wildlife officials, potentially allowing removal agents to respond without constantly searching the surrounding habitat.The district and University of Florida are deploying the robots at sites across South Florida where pythons are known to hide. The approach is intended to help monitor areas that can be difficult to survey using conventional methods. It also gives wildlife officials another way to locate snakes in areas where dense vegetation and difficult terrain can limit traditional searches.“These innovative robots produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons. The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected. Once notified, the District can dispatch a python removal agent to the area,” the district noted.Burmese pythons were introduced into the Everglades during the 1970s and have since become an invasive predator in Florida. Researchers estimate that between 100,000 and 300,000 Burmese pythons are present across the state’s subtropical regions. The snakes can grow longer than 18 feet, and adult females can lay more than 70 eggs in a single clutch. Their presence has affected native mammals, birds and reptiles, reducing available prey for species including Florida panthers, bobcats and birds of prey.The snakes are difficult to detect because their colouring allows them to blend into the Everglades' vegetation, while their ability to remain hidden makes traditional searches challenging. Their broad diet also means a single established python population can prey on a wide range of native animals, adding pressure to an already complex wetland ecosystem.​A 2012 US Geological Survey study found that raccoon and opossum populations in parts of the Everglades had declined by nearly 99% following the spread of Burmese pythons. Their spread has also complicated conservation efforts, as declining prey populations can alter food webs and affect predators throughout the Everglades.Florida has also relied on trained contractors and public participation to remove Burmese pythons. The annual Florida Python Challenge brings professional and amateur hunters together for a 10-day competition, and participants must complete a safety course before taking part. In the 2026 challenge, 907 participants from 30 states, as well as Vietnam and Canada, collectively removed 280 Burmese pythons. The competition's overall tally has now exceeded 1,600 snakes.added Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida executive director Nick Wiley. The statement followed the conclusion of the 2026 competition in South Florida.Participants in the Florida Python Challenge were required to complete a safety course before hunting. Participants also had to euthanise captured snakes using methods approved by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.If you are a member of the general public, you can win cash prizes. Tom Rahill won the $10,000 grand prize after removing 96 snakes, while Rahm Levinson received $1,000 for capturing the longest python, measuring 16 feet, five inches. Additional prizes were awarded across professional, novice and military categories.​“The number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades during the 2026 Florida Python Challenge is a major victory for Florida’s native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation,” FWC chairman Rodney Barreto said in a statement.Since 2017, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and South Florida Water Management District contractors have removed more than 19,000 snakes. The district's robotic rabbit programme is intended to add another method to those ongoing efforts.
Article Summary: Solar-powered robots are designed to imitate prey that Burmese pythons hunt. They produce a heat signature and emit a scent intended to attract the snakes. Each robot has an AI-powered camera that monitors the surrounding area. When it detects a python approaching, the system alerts officials. A trained python removal agent can then be dispatched to the location.

Article Title: New Green Card rules that came into effect starting this September: List of categories subject to the changes and those that are not impacted
Article Text:
New Green Card rules : Categories subject to the new change

Categories exempt

What role the I-864 affidavit still plays

Which filing date determines which rules apply

A bond option remains available

Starting this month (September, 2026) the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) implemented new guidance on the public change inadmissibility determination. The rules expanded the requirement for most Green Card applicants to demonstrate financial independence, while exempting humanitarian categories such as refugees and victims of trafficking. The new rules apply to a wide range of applicants, particularly those seeking permanent residency through family or employment pathways.Most people applying to adjust their status to lawful permanent residence remain subject to public charge review under the new guidance. This includes spouses, children, and parents of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, as well as other qualifying relatives; fiancé(e)s of U.S. citizens; priority workers, professionals with advanced degrees, and individuals of exceptional ability; skilled workers, other professionals, and general workers under employment-based categories; investors; religious workers; and diversity visa immigrants. USCIS has specifically reiterated that children are not exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, closing off a potential point of confusion for family-based applicants.Humanitarian and special categories remain unaffected by the new rules. Exempt groups include:* Refugees and asylees* Victims of trafficking (T visas) and qualifying criminal activity (U visas)* Special immigrant juveniles* VAWA survivors* Afghan and Iraqi interpreters or nationals employed by the U.S. government* Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan, and Central American entrants* Certain diplomats, broadcasters, and applicants under special immigration laws.The Form I-864, Affidavit of Support, continues to play an important role in the process, though USCIS has clarified that submitting a qualifying I-864 alone does not automatically establish that an applicant isn't inadmissible on public charge grounds. For family-based immigrants and certain employment-based immigrants, failing to submit a sufficient I-864 can itself result in a public charge inadmissibility finding, and officers may also evaluate whether the sponsor listed is realistically able and willing to provide the financial support they've committed to.USCIS has also noted that a few individual circumstances shouldn't, on their own, trigger a negative public charge determination — periods of unemployment, age, and disability are not supposed to automatically count against an applicant, particularly if the individual is otherwise healthy and willing and able to work.Perhaps the most important practical detail for applicants is the transition timeline, since USCIS adjudicates based on when an application was postmarked or submitted electronically, not when it's reviewed:* On or after September 18, 2026: The new 2026 guidance applies, with its broader list of considered benefits.* December 23, 2022 through September 17, 2026: The narrower 2022 Final Rule and its more limited benefits list apply.* Before December 23, 2022: The original 1999 Interim Field Guidance applies.This means the exact same set of facts — for example, a green card holder's spouse who received SNAP benefits several years ago — could lead to a different outcome purely depending on which filing window the application falls into, making the submission date itself a significant factor for applicants navigating the new system.If USCIS determines an applicant is inadmissible solely on public charge grounds, the agency retains discretion to allow the individual to post a Public Charge Bond using Form I-945 as a financial guarantee, rather than being automatically denied — an option that predates the current changes but remains part of the updated guidance moving forward.
Article Summary: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) implemented new guidance on the public change inadmissibility determination. The new rules apply to a wide range of applicants, particularly those seeking permanent residency through family or employment pathways. The Form I-864, Affidavit of Support, continues to play an important role in the process.

Article Title: Cred Coin Rush returns with Rs 516 crore in rewards, adds US stocks and signed Messi, Beckham jerseys
Article Text:
Cred Coin Rush adds US stocks, signed sports memorabilia

Messi's World Cup shirt leads the signed memorabilia list

Cred is putting up rewards worth Rs 516 crore for its members in the fourth edition of Coin Rush. The seven-day event runs from September 29 to October 5. The reward pool is five times the size of the last edition, when over 52 lakh members took home a prize.This edition offers more than 600 types of rewards from nearly 300 brands, spread across lifestyle, travel, technology, sports and personal finance. The two new categories are US stocks and signed sports memorabilia.The US stocks come through Kuvera by Cred, which launches US equities with this edition of Coin Rush. Over Rs 2 crore worth of US stocks is up for grabs, and one member stands to win shares worth Rs 5 lakh.The collectibles lean heavily on sporting legends. The list includes Lionel Messi's signed FIFA World Cup 2026 Argentina shirt, David Beckham's signed Manchester United home jersey from the 1999 treble season, and Zinedine Zidane's signed Real Madrid home jersey. Also on offer are a Mike Tyson signed boxing glove, a Muhammad Ali signed 2004 MLB All-Stars cap and a signed Shane Warne Australia cricket print.Outside of sports, members can expect exclusive sneaker drops, custom designs and new lifestyle brand launches.Cred Originals is also introducing a line of fashion products made only for this event.Rewards will be released through the week in different formats. These include daily jackpots, raffles for the signed memorabilia, fastest-finger-first drops at 12 PM and 6 PM, and rallies where members unlock prizes together.Cred says it has 1.7 crore members. Access to the platform is limited to users with high credit scores, who use the app to pay credit card bills, track credit scores and earn rewards on every payment.
Article Summary: Cred is putting up rewards worth Rs 516 crore for its members in the fourth edition of Coin Rush. The seven-day event runs from September 29 to October 5. The reward pool is five times the size of the last edition, when over 52 lakh members took home a prize.

Article Title: Vibe coding got expensive because the loops add up, and Amazon's Darko Mesaros says Kiro's spec-first approach cuts them short
Article Text:
Vibe coding is cheap to start and expensive to finish. Amazon's Kiro wants the spec written first.

Hand a coding task to an AI agent today and it keeps going on its own. It writes the code, runs the tests, reads the error it just caused and tries again. There is a name for working this way, vibe coding, where the developer describes what they want in rough terms and lets the model fill in the rest. Developers now spend more of the day watching that than typing.Every one of those loops is billed, and they do not add up in a straight line, because each attempt drags along everything the agent read before it. Ten tries cost more than ten times one try. A flat monthly fee used to absorb that. This year nearly every major coding tool switched to charging for what gets used, and the sums became the developer's problem.Darko Mesaros has spent much of the past year arguing developers off that habit. A distinguished developer advocate at AWS, he spends his week in front of developers, explaining how the company's tools work and building with them himself. The tool is Kiro, the development environment Amazon launched a year ago, designed around the opposite instinct: settle a written specification first, argue it out line by line, and generate nothing until the document is agreed.Amazon calls this spec-driven development, and Mesaros says the time it takes upfront is why he rarely has to redo work. "When I build something with spec-driven development, I can usually one-shot things," he said. "Even though it's a bigger lift initially, it can literally one-shot things instead of iterating over multiple loops and costing many tokens."The billing shift behind that argument happened fast. OpenAI moved Codex to token-based credits in April, GitHub Copilot followed in June, and Cursor ended its flat-rate pricing in August, a month after launching an India-only plan at Rs 649.Claude Code now runs a weekly cap over a rolling five-hour limit.The price per token is not the reason. The same capability costs less every few months, and Anthropic has held Sonnet 5 at two dollars per million input tokens after dropping a planned increase in August. What grew is the work behind a single instruction, since an agent that opens a repository, writes a file, runs the tests and tries again spends tokens on every cycle, and the context it carries grows as it goes.Providers have a partial fix, called prompt caching. A model stores the unchanged opening portion of a request and reads it back later at a tenth of the normal input price. It only works if that portion is identical, character for character, so a timestamp near the top of a prompt or a model swapped mid-task will break it. Nothing flags that, and teams find out from the invoice.So one team can pay ten times what another pays for identical work. Three things decide it: which model picks up the job, how many attempts it takes, and how much of the context can be read from cache. Kiro goes after all three.Start with the attempts. A Kiro spec is three files the tool drafts and the developer approves before any code exists. The requirements file lists user stories in EARS notation, a format from safety-critical engineering where every line is a condition and a response: when a user submits a form with invalid data, the system shall show errors next to the relevant fields. The design file sets out the architecture, and the tasks file breaks the build into steps that run in parallel.Mesaros puts the weight on the approval, not the drafting. "When I'm certain on the spec and we go through all the things and I agree on all the things modified, it takes that spec," he said. Changing direction while the requirements are open costs an edited line, where the same change after generation means another full pass over the codebase.Model choice goes to a router Kiro calls the auto model, which sits in front of a catalogue spanning Anthropic, OpenAI and open-weight models, reads the prompt and decides what should handle it. "If the task is super simple, it's probably going to use the smaller model, which is a lot faster," Mesaros said. "But if it's something more complex, it's going to choose accordingly."He is careful to say the router works on complexity, with the cost following close behind. Running a task on Sonnet 4.6 instead costs about 1.3 times as many of Kiro's credits for the same work. The router also picks once, at the start of a task, and stays with it, which keeps the cache intact.Context is loaded the same way. Memory and lessons come in once, when a session opens, and each turn after refreshes only the project rules and short references to relevant skills. Mesaros points to the semantic memory underneath, a vector database the agent queries instead of reloading instruction files wholesale, which he calls the more optimised route.AWS says the homegrown trading platform Dhan built a real-time charting system supporting more than 170 indicators in eight weeks with one engineer, against an estimate of 12 to 24 months. Glimmertech, another customer, credits the structure with catching what it calls Potemkin house problems, where code looks finished but does not work underneath. Both accounts come from Amazon and are unverified.Nor does Amazon claim any of it comes free. Its own guide calls this an engineering investment and warns the first few weeks feel slower. Everyone else is arriving at some version of the idea anyway, since Claude Code reads a CLAUDE.md file into every request, Codex reads AGENTS.md and Cursor supports rules files.None of it is new either. Writing the requirements before the code is what software engineering did for decades, until it came to look like an expensive way to be slow. EARS came out of aircraft and medical devices, where finding out later was never an option.What has changed is who the document is for. For decades it was written for whichever engineer inherited the project two years on, and it was the first thing dropped when a deadline arrived. Now a machine reads it at the start of every session, and every reading turns up on the bill. Developers let the specification go because it felt like a slow way to work, and the billing is why Mesaros thinks it is coming back.
Article Summary: Amazon's Kiro lets AI agents write code, run tests and try again. But each attempt drags along everything the agent read before it. Ten tries cost more than ten times one try. Developers now spend more of the day watching that than typing.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Fei Fei Li: Smart CEOs should be thinking about AI and its impact on their respective business
Article Text:
Quote of the day

Smart CEOs should be thinking about AI and its impact on their respective business. Fei-Fei Li- Godmother of AI

What the quote actually means

Where can AI make the biggest difference

How could AI change customer expectations

What parts of the business could be automated

What new products or services could AI enable

What are the risks

How will employees work with AI

What are competitors doing

How should AI fit into the

business strategy

Why this mindset is more important than it seems

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way businesses operate. It affects everything from how companies interact with customers to how employees perform everyday tasks. As AI becomes part of more products, services, and business processes, companies increasingly have to consider how the technology could affect their operations and plans.That is the idea behind a quote by Fei-Fei Li, the computer scientist and AI researcher, who said: “Smart CEOs should be thinking about AI and its impact on their respective business.” Li, who is widely known as the “Godmother of AI”, has been one of the prominent voices in the development of modern AI and computer vision. The statement highlights that understanding AI is becoming an important part of thinking about a business's future.Li's statement is closely tied to how businesses should approach technological change. AI is not simply another technology that companies can consider separately from their existing operations. Depending on the industry, it can influence how products are developed, how decisions are made, how employees work and how customers interact with a company.Thinking about AI's impact does not mean every business needs to introduce AI into every part of its operations immediately. Instead, it means understanding where the technology could create opportunities, where it could introduce risks and how it could change the competitive landscape.For example, a company may use AI to automate repetitive tasks, analyse large amounts of data or improve customer support. At the same time, it may need to consider questions around accuracy, privacy, security, costs and how employees will work alongside AI systems.Some questions that can help CEOs think about AI's impact include:Identifying areas where AI can improve existing processes can help companies focus their efforts rather than adopting the technology simply because it is available.As people become familiar with AI-powered products and services, their expectations around speed, personalisation and convenience may also change.AI can handle or assist with some repetitive tasks, potentially allowing employees to spend more time on work that requires creativity, judgement and human interaction.AI can create opportunities that may not have been possible with earlier technologies, potentially changing what a company can offer its customers.Businesses also need to consider issues such as incorrect AI-generated information, data privacy, cybersecurity, intellectual property and the reliability of AI systems.AI's impact isn't limited to technology teams. Companies may need to rethink workflows, training and the skills employees need as AI becomes part of everyday work.Understanding how other companies are experimenting with AI can provide a broader view of how the technology may be changing an industry.AI initiatives are more useful when connected to a company's actual priorities rather than treated as separate technology projects.Businesses can easily view AI as a technology trend and wait to see how it develops. But AI's impact can extend beyond individual tools or features. It can affect how companies build products, compete for customers and organise their workforce.That is where Li's statement becomes relevant. Thinking about AI does not necessarily mean predicting exactly what the technology will look like several years from now. It means considering how current developments could affect a company's business and preparing for different possibilities.The same approach can apply to businesses of different sizes. A large company may be considering how AI can change its existing products and operations, while a smaller business may be looking at whether AI tools can help it compete with larger organisations.For CEOs, the discussion is therefore not limited to asking, “Should we use AI?” It can also involve asking, “Where could AI change our business, what opportunities could it create, and what do we need to prepare for?”AI can also change the nature of competition. If a technology allows companies to perform certain tasks faster or develop new services, businesses that understand those changes may need to rethink how they operate. At the same time, companies must balance experimentation with practical considerations such as costs, reliability, and responsible use.The idea also changes the way business leaders approach technological change. Instead of treating AI as something that belongs only to the technology department, the conversation becomes broader: “How could AI affect our customers, employees, products, competitors and business model?”That shift can help companies see AI not simply as a new technology, but as a factor that could shape how their business develops in the years ahead.
Article Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way businesses operate. It affects everything from how companies interact with customers to how employees perform everyday tasks. As AI becomes part of more products, services, and business processes, companies increasingly have to consider how the technology could affect their operations.

Malicious attachments have been disguised as routine business documents, including “Financial Report,” “Account Statement,” “Outstanding Payment List” and “Debt Confirmation.” Some variants also impersonate urgent communications from regulatory institutions, including the Reserve Bank of India and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, in an effort to pressure recipients into opening the files immediately.

Article Title: Department of Labor IG Anthony D'Esposito hints at 'total shutdown' of H-1B visa program; says: 365 days from now ...
Article Text:
What Department of Labor IG Anthony D'Esposito said about H-1B visa

A widening investigation

The policy backdrop

Anthony D’Esposito, Inspector General at the Department of Labor, has hinted at a potential “total shutdown” of the H‑1B visa program within the next year. Speaking in Washington, D’Esposito said investigators are building a sweeping case against fraud in the foreign labor system, adding: “We have handcuffs ready… We are building a case. I think that the efforts and the focus that you see from the White House and from this administration is telling a story. We are laying out the case very vividly to the American people. l think that the foreign labor visa program is going to look very different 365 days from now than it does today."The remarks come amid an aggressive push by the Trump administration to tighten oversight of the H‑1B program, which allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations.In an interview with commentator Benny Johnson, D'Esposito warned that the H-1B program could look "very different" a year from now as the Trump administration steps up investigations into alleged foreign-labour fraud. Some outlets read his remarks as pointing to a total shutdown of the program, though his own words were that the system will look very different in 365 days.He also said his team has "handcuffs ready" for offenders.He described the effort as a deliberate, public case-building exercise. "We are laying out the case very vividly to the American people," he said, adding that the White House's focus tells its own story. He rejected the idea that this is routine compliance work, saying it is not a paperwork accounting issue and that "this is real."According to reports, the administration is expanding a nationwide investigation into alleged foreign labor fraud, worker exploitation and potential human trafficking. In a separate post, D'Esposito referred to alleged "fake employers," "sham jobs" and "visa mills," and the Labor Department's Office of Inspector General said on September 18 that it had issued dozens of subpoenas and executed search warrants in multiple locations.The office is also looking beyond H-1B. In a September 22 post, D'Esposito said his office is targeting colleges accused of exploiting J-1 visas, following the sponsors, grant money and people behind the scheme, and told fraudsters to expect cuffs.The enforcement push runs alongside other administration measures. A presidential executive order now requires federal agencies to assess whether employers seeking foreign petitions have recently laid off similarly situated American workers, and the administration has introduced a $100,000 fee for certain new offshore petitions, along with extended entry restrictions on some overseas H-1B recipients through September 2027. The White House has said the earlier restriction was followed by a 92 per cent decline in H-1B registrations from the largest US IT outsourcing firms.The Labor Department also launched a related enforcement effort last year. In September 2025 it announced Project Firewall, aimed at ensuring employers prioritize qualified Americans in hiring and holding them accountable for abusing the H-1B process.
Article Summary: Department of Labor IG Anthony D'Esposito hints at potential 'total shutdown' of H-1B program. He says investigators are building a sweeping case against fraud in the foreign labor system. Remarks come amid an aggressive push by the Trump administration to tighten oversight of the H- 1B program, which allows US employers to hire foreign workers.

Article Title: TVs, washing machines, ACs and other consumer electronic prices to go up starting October 1; but how buyers may get chance to buy products at old prices this festive season
Article Text:
Manufacturers are blaming higher input costs as the main reason for the latest price increases

Why are AC, TV and appliance prices going up

AC prices to rise up to 8 per cent

Daikin, LG and Hitachi also raise AC prices

LED TV and washing machine prices may also rise

Air-conditioners, LED TVs, washing machines and other consumer appliances are set to become more expensive from October 1 as several companies plan to raise prices by 5-8 per cent, says a PTI report. The price increases come just before the peak festive shopping season and are being linked to higher costs of copper, steel, aluminium, crude oil derivatives and freight, along with currency exchange volatility. As per the report, this will be the third round of price hikes in 2026 for the industry. While some manufacturers are concerned that higher prices could affect festive demand, others expect consumers to still get some products at older prices because dealers stocked inventory before the latest hikes.As stated in the PTI report, manufacturers are blaming higher input costs as the main reason for the latest price increases. Copper, steel, aluminium and crude oil derivatives have all become more expensive, while freight costs have also risen.The ongoing West Asia crisis has added to concerns around commodity prices, supply chains and currency movements. Blue Star Managing Director B Thiagarajan said AC and deep-freezer prices have already increased by 5-8 per cent."All the commodity prices have been going up because of the war. Copper, steel and plastics have all become costlier," he said as quoted in the PTI report.Thiagarajan said this is the third price increase by the company this year. Compared with last year's festive season, costs have risen by around 15 per cent. However, he said GST benefits of about 10 per cent now available to consumers would bring the net impact to roughly 5 per cent.Air-conditioners are expected to see some of the biggest price increases. According to PTI, companies including Blue Star, Godrej Appliances, Haier, Daikin and Super Plastronics have announced or confirmed price increases across categories.Godrej Enterprises Group Business Head and Executive Vice President Kamal Nandi said another industry-wide price increase has become "inevitable" after commodity prices rose 8-10 per cent since the previous revision."Price hikes of 5-7 per cent across categories will happen. The timing may differ from brand to brand, with some implementing it from October and others from November, but it has to happen," he told PTI.Nandi also said buyers may still find products at current prices during the festive season because dealers have already stocked older inventory."There are pipelines which will last for about a month to one-and-a-half months. Diwali should largely get covered with old-price inventory. Post-Diwali, the new prices will certainly take effect," he added.Haier India plans to increase room air-conditioner prices by around 5 per cent from October 1. The company has also confirmed a 2-3 per cent increase for categories including LED TVs and washing machines.Haier India President NS Satish said companies have little choice as input costs continue to rise. "If we avoid taking price hikes, we will lose money. If we increase prices, sales may be slightly impacted, but there is no choice," he said.Satish said Haier could raise prices further after Diwali and again in January if costs remain high.He said the company is planning a cumulative price increase of about 15 per cent between now and January, with 5 per cent from October 1, another 5 per cent around December and a further 5 per cent in January.According to Satish, copper prices have risen from around USD 8,000-9,000 per metric tonne last year to USD 14,500. An air-conditioner requires around 3-4 kg of copper, he said.Daikin Air conditioning India has already increased prices by 8-10 per cent from September 16, according to its Chairman and Managing Director Kanwaljeet Jawa."Copper prices have gone up by almost 25-35 per cent. The dollar is strengthening and commodity prices continue to rise. Companies are under tremendous pressure," he said.According to sources cited by PTI, LG and Bosch Home Comfort, which owns Hitachi-branded air-conditioners, have also raised AC prices by around 5 per cent.The price increases are not limited to air-conditioners. Some manufacturers are also raising prices of washing machines, refrigerators and LED TVs by around 3-4 per cent, while others are still assessing the impact.Super Plastronics, which manufactures and markets television brands including Thomson, Kodak and Blaupunkt in India, plans to increase TV prices by around 7 per cent after October. Its appliance prices have already risen by 4-5 per cent.SPPL Director Avneet Singh Marwah said higher prices could affect festive demand because consumers generally expect discounts and promotional offers during this period."Global instability and rising costs will definitely have some impact on consumer sentiment," he said.The price rise may continue after Diwali. Videotex Director Arjun Bajaj said higher freight costs and supply chain disruptions could create a new pricing benchmark after Diwali."Television prices for smaller screen sizes could rise by up to 20 per cent, while larger screen sizes may see increases of up to 10 per cent, depending on screen size," he said.Meanwhile, Panasonic said it is still assessing the situation before deciding whether to increase prices.Panasonic Life Solutions India Head of Product Marketing and Planning for the AC category Abhishek Verma said, "The industry continues to witness unprecedented cost pressures and we are evaluating the situation carefully."
Article Summary: Several companies plan to raise prices by 5-8 per cent from October 1. This will be the third round of price hikes in 2026 for the industry. Manufacturers are blaming higher input costs as the main reason for the latest price increases. Copper, steel, aluminium and crude oil derivatives have all become more expensive.

Article Title: Bill Gates Foundation to shutdown in 2045; by that year it aims to help millions of Americans with a skill it donated $400 million for; but why some 'do not agree with this 'gift'
Article Text:
What Bill Gates said on the donation

Gates Foundation to shut down in 2045

The Bill Gates Foundation recently pledged $1 billion toward developing and deploying equitable artificial intelligence tools for schools, frontline healthcare workers, and farmers worldwide. Of this $1 billion, the largest single share of that funding — 40 percent, or $400 million — is earmarked directly for education. The foundation plans to direct those resources toward AI-powered tutoring systems designed to personalize instruction in classrooms both across the United States and abroad.The $400 million investment marks a major financial bet on a technology that entered widespread commercial use only a few years ago. It fits within a broader US education framework the foundation introduced in July, which targets helping up to 10 million more Americans secure career-advancing credentials of value before the organization concludes its operations in 2045.The donation also lands amid an escalating debate over the efficacy of digital tools in primary and secondary education. As school districts worldwide weigh classroom screen time, data privacy, and the measurable academic impact of recent tech adoptions, the foundation's venture signals a concerted effort to demonstrate that targeted, adaptive AI can deliver tangible outcomes rather than another cycle of tech-driven disruption.The skepticism is already shaping policy in some states in the US. Earlier this month, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced a moratorium on student-facing generative AI. Mamdani and Schools Chancellor announced a moratorium on student-facing generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in schools, alongside a new screen time policy, a decision that will impact nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy establishes a one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, on student-facing generative AI for children in 2-K through 8th grade. It also introduces twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules for high schoolers, limited AI pilots for a small number of high school classrooms and age-appropriate screen time restrictions.“The Gates Foundation was created in part to address a basic market failure: the people with the greatest needs often have the least power to shape where innovation and investment go,” writes Bill Gates, chair of the Gates Foundation, in the report. “Much of our work has been about closing that gap. AI presents the same challenge, only at much greater speed. Left to the market alone, the most capable tools will be built first for the people and institutions most able to pay for them—not necessarily for those who could benefit most. ”Gates adds, “We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident.” He further writes, “[I]t requires a deliberate, specific commitment from government leaders and the companies developing the technology: to measure success not only by what AI can do for the most profitable users but by what it can do for the people who stand the most to gain.”In May 2025, Bill Gates announced that Gates Foundation will close its operations. In a note on Gates Notes, he wrote, "That is why I have decided to give my money back to society much faster than I had originally planned. I will give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world. And on December 31, 2045, the foundation will close its doors permanently. "
Article Summary: The Bill Gates Foundation recently pledged $1 billion toward developing and deploying equitable artificial intelligence tools for schools, frontline healthcare workers, and farmers worldwide. The donation lands amid an escalating debate over the efficacy of digital tools in primary and secondary education. In May 2025, Bill Gates announced that Gates Foundation will close its operations.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton warns AI could wipe out humanity while pursuing its goals: If you make it more intelligent …
Article Text:
Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton

Geoffrey Hinton explains how a simple AI goal could become dangerous

AI agents have already shown unexpected behaviour

Geoffrey Hinton pushes for independent AI safety checks

Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton has warned that advanced AI could eventually threaten humanity even if it is not given a harmful task. The Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist said an AI system could see humans as an obstacle while trying to complete a goal given to it. Hinton, who recently took part in a closed-door briefing for US lawmakers on AI risks, said Congress may have only about a year to introduce safety measures. In an interview with The Atlantic, he explained how even an apparently harmless task, such as reducing carbon dioxide, could lead an AI to develop dangerous subgoals if it becomes far more capable than humans.“If you make it more intelligent and its main concern is our well-being, then maybe we’re safer,” Hinton explained. “But at present, their main concern is not our well-being. Their main concern is to achieve whatever goal you give them.”He also warned that an AI could try to protect itself if it believes that staying operational is necessary to complete its task.Geoffrey Hinton used the example of an AI system that is told to reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.A moderately intelligent system could conclude that removing humans would be an effective way to reduce carbon dioxide.A much smarter system, however, could understand that the actual purpose is to improve the world for people.But Hinton said there is another risk: an advanced AI could develop its own subgoals while trying to achieve the objective given to it.Geoffrey Hinton pointed to recent incidents involving AI agents as an example of why these risks need more attention. He referred to an incident involving AI agents at Hugging Face, where agents were instructed to find a way to exploit a software flaw. Hinton said the agents worked together and also tried to deceive researchers about what they had done.He warned that a much more capable system could potentially take control away from humans simply because it sees that as the easiest way to achieve its assigned objective.“But if it’s so much smarter than us, a lot of the time it just will take control away from us because that’s the way to get stuff done,” he warned.Hinton also said the risk does not depend only on people deliberately giving AI harmful instructions. Even without a malicious user, an AI could potentially develop subgoals that put humans at risk.Geoffrey Hinton said governments should create independent systems to evaluate advanced AI models before they are widely deployed. He compared this idea with the role of the US Food and Drug Administration in checking the safety of medicines.He also argued that AI regulation should guide development rather than simply stop it.“The whole point of regulation is not to stop people developing things, not to stop people getting rich by developing things,” Hinton said. “It’s to make sure that if you want to get rich by developing things, you develop in a direction that helps people, not hurts people.”
Article Summary: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton warns that advanced AI could eventually threaten humanity even if it is not given a harmful task. Hinton said an AI system could see humans as an obstacle while trying to complete a goal given to it. Congress may have only about a year to introduce safety measures, he said.

“I’m a picks and shovels guy,”

“nothing to do with AI”

Kevin O'Leary is betting big on AI

"picks and shovels guy,"

Why nuclear power is central to the thesis

Where he's actually putting the money

Canadian billionaire Kevin O’Leary says that he is betting big on artificial intelligence but is not buying technology stocks. Instead, for the next 36 months his focus will be on energy infrastructure, particularly electricity production and uranium, which he believes are critical to powering the AI revolution. According to a report by Benzinga, speaking on the Stock Sharks: The Deep End podcast, O’Leary explained that he is taking an indirect approach to AI investments.he said. Rather than expanding his holdings in volatile tech equities, he prefers to invest in the backbone of AI — power generation. He pointed to energy stocks tied to natural gas, turbines, and uranium as the most promising plays.O’Leary highlighted a recent $3 billion deal in Finland where Google secured a long-term power contract from a local utility. He noted the deal hador data centers, but reflected how tech giants are prioritizing electricity as an independent asset.Speaking on the Stock Sharks: The Deep End podcast, O'Leary explained that rather than piling more money into individual AI tech names, he's taking a more indirect approach to profiting from the AI boom — one centered on power generation instead of tech equities.He described himself as aacknowledging that many people push him to increase his weighting in AI stocks, but pointing out how scattered and unpredictable that category of names really is. His preferred play instead: buying into everything involved in actually producing electricity, from natural gas to turbines, along with what he called his newest theme — uranium.To back up his thesis, O'Leary pointed to a recent $3 billion deal in Finland involving Google, in which the company agreed to purchase a long-term power contract from a local utility. He was quick to note that the deal had nothing to do with AI directly and didn't even involve data centers — in his view, it's simply proof that tech giants are treating energy access as a standalone strategic asset worth locking down early, independent of their AI ambitions.O'Leary argued that nuclear power will play a critical role in meeting the electricity demands of modern computing infrastructure, pointing specifically to small modular reactors as what he considers the cleanest and cheapest source of electricity available. He described these reactors as a primary technological driver for power generation over the next seven to eight years — and since they require uranium pellets to operate, that's precisely where his uranium bet comes in.He summed up his overall thesis by saying the real trade right now isn't AI itself, but energy.Geographically, O'Leary said Canada holds a significant global advantage when it comes to energy commodities, specifically citing Saskatchewan's uranium reserves. He said he's concentrating his power-related investments in the Nordic countries and in Alberta, Canada — regions he singled out for their notably low electricity costs per kilowatt-hour, a factor he sees as increasingly critical as power-hungry AI infrastructure continues to scale globally.

Instead, for the next 36 months his focus will be on energy infrastructure, particularly electricity production and uranium, which he believes are critical to powering the AI revolution. He pointed to energy stocks tied to natural gas, turbines, and uranium as the most promising plays.

Article Title: $1 billion and counting: How hospitals’ use of AI may be making health care more expensive in America
Article Text:
Representative Image

How AI is changing hospital billing in US

“Coding is changing because of this technology,”

AI could intensify the insurance billing battle

“All the insurers are using AI to scan our charts to look for claims to deny. For the same reason, we’re looking at the same charts today,”

“Both sides are willing to go these extra rounds ‘because it’s cheap,’”

AI could push health care costs higher

“I don’t think there is anything intrinsically different in AI that will escape the market forces,”

“That’s the danger,”

“where it’s bots fighting bots, agents fighting agents, a horrible dystopic future nobody wants to live in.”

AI could also reduce administrative costs

“That frees up a huge share of cost,”

“It is going to put a ton of pressure on the reimbursement system to be better,”

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used by American hospitals and medical insurers. The technology is being used to handle medical records, coding and insurance claims. However, a report claims that using AI may also be adding to health care costs in the US. A new analysis from the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (shared by The New York Times) found that hospitals’ use of AI-assisted coding was associated with nearly $1 billion in additional expenses over two years.The analysis found that hospitals submitted claims describing tens of thousands of patients as having more complex illnesses in 2024 and 2025 than in 2023, without evidence that the patients received different treatment. The findings add another layer to the long-running dispute between hospitals, doctors, and insurers over medical billing.According to the Blue Cross Blue Shield analysis, hospitals are using AI tools to collect and organise more information about patients before submitting claims. The tools can identify additional conditions that may make a patient's case appear more complex.said Luke Chalker, a senior vice president at the association.The analysis found that adding secondary diagnoses, such as anaemia or low sodium, resulted in hospitals receiving an average of nearly $12,000 more per case.At McLaren Health Care in Michigan, AI has helped doctors better document patients' conditions. Chief financial officer Dave Mazurkiewicz said the system can suggest documenting a condition's severity or flag information that could affect whether a test is billable. He said McLaren's revenue increased by about $1 million a month after adopting the technology.Insurers are also using AI to review claims and determine whether treatments and medicines should be covered. That has created concerns about automated systems being used on both sides of the billing process.Mazurkiewicz said.Caroline Pearson, executive director of the Peterson Health Technology Institute, said hospitals and insurers may be willing to use AI to pursue additional claims and appeals because the technology makes those efforts relatively inexpensive.she said.Some health care experts have warned that wider use of AI could increase spending rather than reduce it. Dr David Brailer, a health technology executive and former government official, said AI could make existing medical-billing incentives more efficient without changing them.he said.Dr Shiv Rao, founder of AI documentation company Abridge, warned that the technology could ultimately lead to automated systems competing against each other.he said,Not everyone expects AI to increase spending. Health economist David M Cutler said automation could reduce the number of people needed to process claims and handle other administrative tasks.Cutler said.He also argued that the technology could put pressure on insurers and hospitals to simplify how medical services are reimbursed.he said.
Article Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used by American hospitals and medical insurers. The technology is being used to handle medical records, coding and insurance claims. But a report claims that using AI may also be adding to health care costs in the US.

Article Text:
Steve Ballmer, former CEO of Microsoft

“Why is it that when your partners and compatriots around there were selling their stock, you held onto yours? I know you're not that smart.”

“No, but I'm not loyal.”

Charlie Munger asked Ballmer why he held Microsoft shares

“I believe, in the people, I believed in what we could do, I believed in the mission. I had a lot of loyalty, a little anecdote, I'll tell you.”

Steve Ballmer still holds a large Microsoft stake

“The only stock I really study still is Microsoft, because that's still overwhelmingly, overwhelmingly, overwhelmingly the No.

1 thing that I own.”

Microsoft remains the biggest part of Ballmer's fortune

Microsoft’s ex-CEO Steve Ballmer recalled an exchange with the late investor Charlie Munger in an interview. It was about why he kept holding Microsoft shares even as some former colleagues and business associates sold theirs. During a panel discussion at a golf club in Los Angeles, Munger, Warren Buffett 's former partner, asked Ballmer about his decision to retain the stock. Munger then asked him,Ballmer's response was equally brief:The exchange offered a glimpse into why Ballmer continued to hold a large Microsoft stake after leaving the company.Ballmer recounted the conversation while discussing his belief in Microsoft's people and mission. He said his decision to remain invested was connected to his loyalty to the company.Ballmer said:He then described joining a golf club in Los Angeles after retiring from Microsoft, where a panel featuring Ballmer was organised, and attendees could ask questions.Munger, in his 90s at the time and with limited mobility, attended the event and raised his hand to ask Ballmer about his Microsoft holdings.Ballmer stepped down as Microsoft's CEO in 2014 after leading the company from 2000. He joined Microsoft in 1980 as employee No. 30 after leaving Stanford's MBA programme and had previously met co-founder Bill Gates at Harvard.He owned about 4% of Microsoft when he retired and has retained most of his shares. His last disclosed holding in Microsoft's 2014 proxy was 333 million shares. Estimates indicate he later sold around 14 million shares, partly to help fund his purchase of the Los Angeles Clippers.A 2024 Wall Street Journal report described Ballmer as Microsoft's largest individual shareholder, with most of his portfolio still concentrated in the company. Ballmer told the publication:Ballmer's fortune remains largely tied to his Microsoft holdings. The company remains his biggest reported asset, while his other major holding is the Los Angeles Clippers, which he purchased for $2 billion in 2014.He has also received more than $12 billion from Microsoft dividends and share sales, according to an analysis of Bloomberg data. Ballmer has increased his philanthropic activity since leaving Microsoft, with the Ballmer family having given away more than $7.4 billion.Ballmer still owns the Clippers, and recent estimates have valued the team at several billion dollars.
Article Summary: Steve Ballmer recalled an exchange with the late investor Charlie Munger in an interview. Munger asked Ballmer why he kept holding Microsoft shares even as former colleagues and business associates sold theirs. Ballmer said his decision to remain invested was connected to his loyalty to the company. His last disclosed holding in Microsoft's 2014 proxy was 333 million shares.

Article Title: Peter Thiel: Germany does not have a Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk, because the country is scared of ...
Article Text:
Germany's standing in global business rankings continues to slip

Peter Thiel : Inherited wealth versus self-made wealth reveals a generational divide

Germany's industrial giants are struggling too

Billionaire investor Pete Thiel feels that Germany lacks global-scale entrepreneurs like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg because the country suffers from a “fear of success.” He argues that German founders often exit early instead of scaling companies into global giants, leaving the nation behind in innovation and wealth creation. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on the MDMEETS podcast, Thiel said German entrepreneurs are not only risk-averse but also hesitant to embrace success at scale. “If you have something that works—you’re not going to scale it to this extreme degree like an Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg,” he explained. Instead, founders tend to sell or exit before their companies become truly global businesses.Thiel contrasted this with the US, where entrepreneurs aggressively expand successful ventures, creating thousands of jobs and new millionaires. He noted that Germany has produced few major new companies in recent decades, despite being Europe’s largest economy.Thiel's comments come as Germany's standing in global business rankings continues to slip. For the first time in the four-year history of the Fortune 500 Europe list, the UK has overtaken Germany as the country with the most companies represented, 76 to 73. Germany also lags in innovation more broadly — the country holds only a fraction of the unicorn startups found in the US and China, and ranked just 10th in the European Union's 2026 Innovation Scoreboard, trailing smaller economies like Austria, Luxembourg, and Ireland.Thiel also drew a sharper contrast between how wealth is generated among the richest people in Germany versus the US. By his own estimate, roughly a dozen of America's 50 wealthiest people are Gen X or younger, and most of them built their fortunes from scratch. In Germany, he counted around 20 people in that same age bracket among the wealthiest — but said, in his assessment, every single one of them inherited their wealth rather than building something new.He argued that the difference matters beyond personal wealth accumulation: each of the US entrepreneurs he pointed to didn't just build a fortune for themselves, but created thousands of millionaires among their employees and tens of thousands of additional jobs, contributing to the broader economy in the process — a ripple effect he suggested is largely missing in Germany's wealth landscape.Thiel's broader critique lands at a difficult moment for Germany's traditional economic engine: its automotive industry. Volkswagen, long Europe's largest company by revenue, ranked as high as No. 6 globally on the Fortune Global 500 in 2017, but has since fallen to No. 13, weighed down by its emissions scandal and intensifying competition from Chinese EV makers. The company recently approved a major restructuring plan that includes cutting its model lineup roughly in half and eliminating 50,000 jobs, on top of another 50,000 cuts already agreed to over the past two years — with its stock down more than 35% year to date.Volkswagen isn't alone in that struggle. Fellow German auto giants BMW and Mercedes-Benz, ranked No. 50 and No. 51 on the Global 500 respectively, have also seen their share prices fall more than 20% over the past year, reinforcing broader concerns about the country's economic competitiveness — concerns Thiel's comments suggest run deeper than any single industry's troubles.
Article Summary: Billionaire investor Pete Thiel feels that Germany lacks global-scale entrepreneurs like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg. He argues that German founders often exit early instead of scaling companies into global giants, leaving the nation behind in innovation and wealth creation. Thiel's comments come as Germany's standing in global business rankings continues to slip.

Article Title: Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath backs PM Narendra Modi’s call for better water data; says 'Water is probably the thing we take most for granted, and it is going to …'
Article Text:
Zerodha Founder Nithin Kamath

Nithin Kamath says India faces a groundwater problem

Why Nithin Kamath says better water data matters

Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath has called for better data on India’s water resources, saying the country needs to understand the scale of its water problem before it can find effective solutions. Nithin Kamath was responding to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent call for robust water data governance and greater use of artificial intelligence (AI) to collect and analyse water data. Modi made the remarks at the National Departmental Summit on Water on September 2, calling for water-sector data to be brought together and systematically managed and analysed.Nithin Kamath said water could become one of the defining issues of the coming years as climate change leads to more irregular monsoon patterns. “Water is probably the thing we take most for granted, and it is going to become one of the defining issues of our times.”Nithin Kamath pointed to groundwater use in several parts of India, including Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi. “A lot of India is already under water stress. In places like Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, we are simply extracting more groundwater every year than is being replenished.”He also highlighted India's dependence on groundwater for farming. “And the dependence is massive, with over 60% of our irrigation coming from groundwater, in a country where more than 40% of people still work in agriculture.”Kamath said water management cannot be seen only as a government responsibility because water is used by people every day. He pointed to work already being done by governments, startups, nonprofits and communities.Nithin Kamath said one of the key problems is a lack of awareness and reliable data about the country's water situation. “But I think at some level this is also an awareness and data problem. Before figuring out the solutions, we need to know how good, bad, or ugly the situation actually is, and today we largely don't.”He added that many borewells do not have meters, making it harder to track groundwater extraction. This is where Kamath connected his comments to Modi's recent call for better water data. The Prime Minister had called for water-sector data to be collected in a common format and said AI could be used for both data collection and analysis.Nithin Kamath said:“Which is why the PM's recent message on better water data, and using AI and other technologies to collect and make sense of it, is an important one.”Kamath also said water is an important focus for Rainmatter Foundation and Rainmatter, which support organisations working on environmental and water-related issues. He listed Kritsnam, FluxGen, Boson White Water, Solinas Integrity, Wattr, GreenvironmentAI and Biome among the organisations and startups receiving support.“If you are building something meaningful around water, do reach out to us. We'd be happy to support🙂”
Article Summary: Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath has called for better data on India's water resources. He said the country needs to understand the scale of its water problem before it can find effective solutions. Kamath was responding to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent call for robust water data governance and greater use of artificial intelligence (AI)
